concept: Why do predator and prey populations rise and fall in cycles?
title: The Valley of the Endless Chase
tagline: Two populations, one rhythm — what makes them dance?

science.hiddenLaw: Lotka-Volterra predator-prey coupling: dN/dt = rN - aNP and dP/dt = e·aNP - mP, producing sustained neutral cycles where prey abundance drives predator growth with a time lag and prey peaks precede predator peaks by ~1/4 period.
science.plainStatement: Prey increase when predators are rare and decrease when predators are common; predators increase when prey are common and decrease when prey are rare. Because each population's growth depends on the other, they chase each other in repeating cycles with prey peaking first and predators peaking later.
misconceptions: Predator and prey peaks occur at the same time (synchronous cycles) — in fact prey peaks lead predator peaks by a quarter-period lag.
Cycles are caused by external seasonal or environmental forcing — in fact they are internally generated by the trophic interaction itself even in constant environments.
Predators will inevitably eat prey to extinction — in fact the coupled system produces sustained oscillations, not extinction, under classic conditions.

Increasing prey intrinsic growth rate (more food for prey) increases mean prey abundance — in fact it increases mean predator abundance (P* = r/a) while mean prey stays set by predator traits (N* = m/(e·a)).

story.setting: A secluded alpine valley where hares and lynx have been counted for decades. The ranger's cabin holds logbooks filled with wavy lines, and the meadow looks the same year after year — same grass, same snowmelt, same quiet forest.
story.mystery: Why do hare and lynx numbers rise and fall in repeating waves, with hare booms always followed a little later by lynx booms, even though the weather and seasons stay perfectly steady?
story.goal: Tune the valley's hidden dials — how fast hares breed, how often lynx hunt, how well hunts turn into new lynx — and watch the living waves. Find what controls the rhythm and what really sets the averages.

predictions.prompt: You start with 60 hares and 10 lynx and watch for many cycles in a constant environment. How will the peaks line up?
options: Hare and lynx peaks occur at exactly the same time
Hare peaks occur first, lynx peaks follow after a delay
Lynx peaks occur first, hare peaks follow after a delay
Peaks occur randomly with no consistent order

predictions.prompt: Some visitors say the ups and downs must be caused by seasons or weather. You keep temperature, rain and food perfectly constant. What happens to the cycles?
options: Cycles disappear and both populations stay flat
Cycles continue with the same predator-prey chase
Both populations crash to extinction
Prey explodes while predators disappear

predictions.prompt: A ranger worries lynx will eat all hares and then starve. Starting from 40 hares and 9 lynx, what actually happens over many years?
options: Hares are eaten to extinction and lynx then starve
Both populations settle into repeating cycles and persist
Both populations grow forever without limit
Lynx disappear and hares grow unchecked

predictions.prompt: You fertilize the meadow so hares can breed faster (higher growth rate). After many cycles, what happens to the long-term averages?
options: Average hares increase a lot, average lynx stays the same
Average lynx increase a lot, average hares stay about the same
Both averages increase equally
Both averages decrease

transfer.setup: A tank holds tiny drifting plants and the animals that eat them. The light and the temperature never change. There are no seasons. You can add food so the plants grow faster.
transfer.question: You add enough food for the plants to grow much faster. Over a long time, what happens to the average numbers?
options: More plants on average, and the same number of animals
More animals on average, and the same number of plants
Both grow a lot, on average
Both die out

checks.description: With standard Lotka-Volterra parameters both populations show sustained oscillations with large normalized amplitude
Prey peaks precede predator peaks by a positive lag (quarter period), not simultaneous
Instantaneous zero-lag correlation between prey and predator is not strongly positive, refuting synchrony misconception
Higher prey intrinsic growth rate raises mean predator abundance as P* = r/a
Mean prey abundance stays at N* = m/(e*a) ~100 regardless of prey growth rate, refuting more-food-more-prey misconception
Control: removing predation eliminates cycles - prey oscillation amplitude collapses
